title: What Actually Is an IP Address?
sources: ARIN blog, 'The IANA IPv4 Free Pool has Depleted' (arin.net/blog/2011/02/03/iana-ipv4-free-pool-depletion): on 3 Feb 2011 IANA allocated the last remaining IPv4 /8 blocks to the regional registries
IPv4 uses 32-bit addresses: 2^32 = about 4.3 billion, written as four numbers 0-255 separated by dots (dotted decimal), e.g. 192.168.1.5 (RFC 791; NRO 'IPv4 - where are we now')

Computerworld, 'FAQ: What you need to know about IPv6': IPv6 uses 128-bit addresses, about 340 undecillion (3.4 x 10^38); divided by ~8.2 billion people that is ~4 x 10^28 each = trillions of trillions

Network Academy 'Why do we need NAT' / ipfyi 'NAT explained': a home router shares one public IP address among all devices, giving each a private address (192.168.x.x, RFC 1918) and translating with NAT
MaxMind 'IP geolocation accuracy': an IP address maps only to an approximate area (country/city), not a person or street address

lines.text: What actually is an IP address?
It's like a home address for your phone,
so data knows exactly where to go.
It's just four numbers with dots in between.
When you open a video, your request carries that address,
lines.caps: WHEN YOU *OPEN | A *VIDEO | YOUR *REQUEST | CARRIES THAT *ADDRESS

lines.text: so the reply finds its way back to you.
lines.caps: SO THE *REPLY | FINDS ITS *WAY | BACK TO *YOU

lines.text: there are only about four billion of them,
and the last free blocks were handed out in twenty eleven.
lines.caps: AND THE *LAST | FREE *BLOCKS | WERE HANDED *OUT | IN *2011

lines.text: So your whole home shares one public address,
and your router hands each device a private one.
lines.caps: AND YOUR *ROUTER | HANDS EACH *DEVICE | A *PRIVATE ONE

lines.text: The real fix is I P v six,
with trillions of trillions for every person alive.
It's not who you are, just where you are.
